Recycled PA (rPA): properties, applications and benefits Materials we offer Ambio for Recyclers About us Request a quote Menu Materials we offer Ambio for Recyclers About us Request a quote Recycled polyamide (rPA): properties, applications and benefits Can PA be recycled? Yes. Recycled Polyamide (rPA) is an engineering thermoplastic recovered from post-consumer (PCR) and post-industrial (PIR) waste, such as production scrap, carpet fibre, fishing nets and automotive parts. It keeps virgin polyamide's strength, wear resistance and heat resistance. The common grades are PA6 and PA66 (PA6.6), often glass-filled for technical parts. Request a quote What are the key properties of recycled PA? Physical properties of rPA Unfilled recycled PA has a density of about 1.13 to 1.15 g/cm³; glass-filled grades are heavier. Polyamide absorbs moisture, which changes its stiffness and toughness and means it must be dried before processing. Mechanical properties of rPA rPA offers high tensile strength, toughness, fatigue resistance and excellent abrasion resistance. Dry, unfilled PA can be notch sensitive; conditioned or impact-modified grades are tougher. PA66 is stiffer and more heat resistant than PA6, and glass fibre raises both further. Chemical properties of rPA Recycled PA resists oils, greases, fuels and many solvents, but is attacked by strong acids. PA66 melts at around 260 °C and PA6 at around 220 °C, so both work at elevated temperatures. Recycled PA6 and PA66 compounds serve many of these parts; the most demanding under-the-hood components need tightly specified, heat-stabilised grades, which is where batch testing matters most. rPA in textiles and fibres Textiles use rPA in sportswear, swimwear, hosiery and carpet fibre, much of it regenerated from nets and fibre waste. rPA in consumer and industrial goods rPA goes into power tool and appliance housings, furniture parts, gears, rollers, bearings and other wear parts. What are the benefits of using recycled PA? Environmental benefits rPA reduces waste and greenhouse gas emissions compared with virgin polyamide, whose production is energy intensive, and keeps material such as nets and fibre out of landfill and the sea. Economic benefits Recycled PA can cost less than virgin PA for the same part, and helps manufacturers meet recycled-content targets. Performance benefits Compounding with glass fibre, impact modifiers, heat stabilisers and flame retardants tunes rPA for demanding applications. PA6, PA66 and nylon What is the difference between PA6 and PA66? PA66 has a higher melting point, stiffness and heat resistance, suiting high-temperature parts. PA6 is easier to process, slightly tougher and usually cheaper. What is the difference between PA and nylon? They are the same family: nylon is a common trade name for polyamides. PA covers PA6, PA66 and others, used both as fibres and as engineering plastics. Request a quote Frequently asked questions about recycled PA How does recycled PA compare to virgin PA? Good rPA compounds perform similarly to virgin PA in many applications. Quality depends on feedstock, processing and compounding, and on moisture control. What are the challenges of using recycled PA? Moisture absorption, variation between batches and degradation from prior processing. Drying, restabilising and batch testing address them. Can recycled PA be recycled again? Yes, several times, though properties change gradually over repeated cycles. Is recycled PA toxic? Recycled PA is considered safe under normal use, though traces of additives or residual monomers may be present. Testing and compliance with REACH keep it within safety requirements. Is recycled PA biodegradable? No. Like virgin polyamide, it does not readily break down; recycling extends its lifespan. Where can I buy recycled PA?
